newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan pro-independence party not to embrace China.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan pro-independence party not to embrace China.

text.p: Taiwan's main opposition Democratic Progressive Party on Tuesday risked provoking China by declaring that it had no intention of embracing unification with the mainland.

The comment came after a newspaper report that the party had abandoned its pro-independence cause to identify itself with the Nationalist government, which has a policy of eventual reunification with China.

"Our stance is clear, that is, Taiwan is never a part of the People's Republic of China, and we have no intention at all to embrace unification with the mainland," Yen Wan-chin, acting director of the party's China Affairs Department, told Reuters.
"It is an undeniable fact that Taiwan has long been independent. Although the Chinese communists are reluctant to accept this, they have no way to change such a fact," Yen said.
Taiwan and China split after a civil war in 1949, which saw the defeated Nationalists fleeing the mainland.
Beijing, which still regards Taiwan as a renegade province, has threatened to attack Taiwan if it declares independence.

Yen criticized the vice chairman of the government's National Development Conference, Vincent Siew, for trying to distort the opposition party's stance to placate China and ease tension between Taipei and Beijing.

He was referring to Siew's comment quoted by the United Daily News on Tuesday that the Democratic Progressive Party had agreed to drop its pro-independence stance during a state-sponsored conference last month.
Siew later told reporters he meant only that the opposition party agreed with the government stance that the existence of the Republic of China, Taiwan's official title, was most important.

Relations between Taipei and Beijing, never cordial, soured further after Taiwanese President Lee Teng-hui visited the United States in June 1995 in a trip interpreted by Beijing as an attempt to promote independence.
China later suspended semi-official talks with the island and staged war games to try to intimidate Taiwan.
